analysis.one_liner: Ends patent giveaways of federal mining land and makes hardrock miners pay royalties and cleanup fees for the first time.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on November 5, 2015 and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill overhauls the Mining Law of 1872, which still governs gold, silver, copper, and other hardrock mining on federal land. It would stop selling federal land to mining claim holders, charge companies an annual fee for each claim, and impose the first-ever federal royalty of 2 to 5 percent on hardrock minerals taken from public land, plus a fee of up to 2 percent of production value to clean up abandoned mines. It would also require mining permits, reclamation plans, and bonds so companies—not taxpayers—restore the land and water they disturb.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of Western mining states and tribal lands living near abandoned hardrock mines, many of which leak acid mine drainage into streams and groundwater; taxpayers, who have historically absorbed cleanup costs and received no royalties for minerals taken from public land; and hunters, anglers, and outdoor users whose watersheds and habitats would be restored.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Western and tribal communities near abandoned mines

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a Hardrock Minerals Reclamation Fund, financed by a 0.6 to 2 percent fee on production, to reclaim abandoned mines in fourteen Western states and on Indian land, prioritizing protection of public health and safety and treatment of abandoned-mine water pollution.

Imposes the first federal royalty on hardrock mining—2 to 5 percent of gross income—so taxpayers share in the value of minerals taken from public land, along with $150 annual maintenance fees and $50 location fees per claim.
Prohibits new patents—outright sales of federal land for roughly $5 per acre—except for applications filed by September 30, 1994, ending a 19th-century land-disposal practice.

Requires exploration and mining permits, financial assurances (bonds) sized to actual cleanup costs, and restoration of land and water to a condition capable of supporting their prior uses, with quarterly inspections and civil and criminal penalties for violations.

Directs federal land managers to review wilderness study areas, roadless areas, and lands near national parks, monuments, and wild and scenic rivers, and to withdraw the most vulnerable lands from mining.

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies operating on federal land, which would pay royalties and production fees for the first time, annual claim fees, land-use fees, and reclamation bonds; some of those costs could reach consumers through higher mineral prices, and new permitting requirements could slow domestic exploration and mine development.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hardrock mining companies on federal land

drawbacks.text: New royalties, fees, and bonding requirements would raise production costs for miners on federal land, which could discourage domestic exploration and production—the bill itself requires Interior to report every five years on any impact on domestic exploration and production.

The bill grandfathered existing operations: no royalty applies to mines already producing under an approved plan of operations on the date of enactment, so the industry's largest current mines would have kept extracting royalty-free.

The royalty and reclamation fee are ranges that Interior sets by regulation, and Interior could reduce or waive royalties where a company shows production would not otherwise occur—leaving room for the rates to be set or reduced leniently.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill imposed real, but conventional, costs on an industry that—alone among major extractive industries—pays no federal royalty for hardrock minerals taken from public land and can still patent that land. The cleanup fund, bonding, and permit requirements target hazards like acid mine drainage that otherwise become public health problems and taxpayer burdens. The main honest concerns are permitting cost and possible effects on domestic mineral supply, and the bill's own grandfathering and royalty-relief provisions softened the industry impact considerably. On balance the design favors the public, with meaningful transition protections for the industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where it sat without a hearing or a vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Udall introduced the Hardrock Mining and Reclamation Act of 2015 on November 5, 2015, joined by four Democratic colleagues: Senators Heinrich, Bennet, Wyden, and Markey.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources that same day.
The bill received no further action—no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote—before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies came out ahead: they continue to extract gold, silver, copper, and other minerals from federal land without paying any federal royalty, and residents near abandoned mines continue to live with the contamination and cleanup costs the fund would have addressed.

for.name: Sen. Tom Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship.

for.name: Sens. Martin Heinrich, Michael Bennet, Ron Wyden, and Ed Markey
for.role: U.S. Senators from New Mexico, Colorado, Oregon, and Massachusetts
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only four cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee chaired by Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK); referred the bill's sole destination
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it received no action after referral for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Hardrock mining industry
against.role: Industry operating under the Mining Law of 1872
against.what_they_did: Long opposed federal royalties and patent limits for hardrock mining on public land; no mining-reform bill advanced in this committee.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill died in the Republican-chaired Energy and Natural Resources Committee without ever reaching a roll-call vote, so no vote-based partisan split exists in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have ended their century-old exemption from federal royalties, charged annual claim fees, required reclamation bonds, and cut off new patent purchases of federal land. Its interest ran against the public's, since its savings came from extracting public minerals and leaving cleanup costs behind.

The bill's Reclamation Fund would finance large-scale cleanup of abandoned mines by states, tribes, federal agencies, and grantees, creating reclamation work while addressing public health hazards like mine drainage.
They would pay new $150 maintenance and $50 location fees, but holders of ten or fewer claims who performed their assessment work were exempted from the maintenance fee.
